title: Short Stuff: Dagen H
summary: Short Stuff episode on Dagen H (Swedish "H-Day"), the day on September 3, 1967 when Sweden switched from driving on the left to driving on the right. Covers the name's meaning (Dagen H, "högertrafik" / right-hand traffic), Sweden's long history of left-side driving since 1734, the public information campaign (pamphlets, TV/radio/newspaper ads, logo, theme song contest), the song "Håll dig till höger" by the Telestars, the infrastructure overhaul (street signs, buses, traffic lights), a 1955 referendum voters rejected, the rationale of car design and safety, the overnight switch with roughly 360,000 signs changed, the cost, and post-switch fatality trends leading to Vision Zero.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts open the show, joke about a pig Latin-style phrase, and introduce the topic of Dagen H, Sweden's switch to right-hand traffic.

segments.title: What Dagen H means and the 1967 switch
segments.summary: Explains that Dagen H means H-Day, with H standing for högertrafik (right-hand traffic). The switch occurred on September 3, 1967, ending left-side driving that dated to 1734.

segments.title: Public information campaign and theme song
segments.summary: Describes the public information campaign: a pamphlet explaining how to drive on the right, TV, radio and newspaper ads, a logo, and a song contest for a theme song. The winning song, Håll dig till höger by the Telestars, reached number five on the Swedish charts; its title also carried a joke about fidelity.

segments.title: Infrastructure changes and reasons for the switch
segments.summary: Covers the infrastructure overhaul (street signs, bus stops, traffic lights, bike lanes, one-way streets, bus doors) and the 1955 referendum voters rejected. Reasons included Sweden lagging behind the rest of the world and cars with left-side steering, such as Volvos, being designed for right-side driving.

segments.title: The overnight changeover and its cost
segments.summary: Traffic was shut down the day before and day of; about 360,000 street signs were changed in under 24 hours. Switch happened at 4:50 a.m. on September 3 with a radio countdown. No fatalities the next day and a slightly below-normal number of crashes on Monday. Cost was about 6 million kronor, roughly 5 million over budget.

segments.title: Aftermath and Vision Zero
segments.summary: Fatalities rose again within a couple of years as people adjusted. Sweden later launched Vision Zero to eliminate traffic deaths regardless of side of road; fatalities were down to 270 in 2016.

segments.title: Sign-off and Invisible recommendation
segments.summary: Hosts recommend the Invisible podcast, which covers the topic with interviews from people who were there, and sign off.
